---
title: "Silent Sunday"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-06-21"
draft: yes
categories: [observance]
---

Compared to the United States during the 1970s, current Sunday has not only become another weekday in terms of shopping, but it has become the go-to day for relaxation, consumerism, and entertainment.

The quiet, empty landscapes of my childhood have been replaced by first the high traffic of malls that transitioned to mail order deliveries that became a seven-day-a-week commerce.

It raises a fundamental question for our modern lives: when every day is treated as a special day, when do we actually rest and worship?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

When my family first arrived in Maryland, our surrounding area was small and our resources were scarce.

We lived inside the Capital Beltway (I-495), had no car, and relied entirely on our own feet to get to school and to carry groceries home from the A&P.

Because of those physical limitations, our week had a natural rhythm.

We had to plan ahead.

Shopping was a chore done "prior to the Sabbath," because we knew that once Sunday arrived, there would be no open stores.

In those days, closing doors on Sundays was a collective cultural pause.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

That silence provided a protective boundary.

Because the world outside our apartment walls refused to transact business, we were insulated from the temptation to constantly produce or consume.

We didn't have to choose between keeping up with the world or keeping the Sabbath holy—the world itself was resting.

It was within that quiet space that our family established its spiritual routine, anchoring ourselves in church community and family closeness without the competing noise of the marketplace.

Today, that collective boundary has completely dissolved. The modern world is engineered for friction-free, perpetual motion.

If we need something, we buy it instantly on a screen.

If we are bored, an endless loop of entertainment is waiting for us, seven days a week, twenty-four hours a day. The deliberate margin that once protected our souls has been paved over by convenience.

But when we treat every day with the same casual, high-speed intensity, we lose the capacity for deep renewal. We mistake amusement for rest, and distraction for worship.

The contrast between the silent Sundays of the 1970s and the chaotic Sundays of today reminds me that holiness requires a boundary.

If the world will no longer provide that pause for us structurally, we have to build it ourselves internally.

We have to learn the discipline of closing our own digital doors, setting down our baskets, and stepping away from the commerce of the world—reclaiming the quiet hours where we can finally stop doing, and remember who we are.
